paras: The lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French took place at Los Lunas, New Mexico, in early March 1882, when masked men took the three prisoners from the jail and hanged them from the nearest trees. The same mob took two Black prisoners from the jail, beat them and turned them loose. The story spread nationwide through an Albuquerque special to the Denver Republican, which presented the three hanged men as murderers.

According to the Albuquerque dispatch, the three hanged men were jail prisoners, each accused of a separate killing. Shelton was said to have murdered a foreman named Woodruff the previous fall, and Redmond to have killed James McDermott the previous January at Gallup, on the Atlantic and Pacific railway. French, also known as Simpson, was described as one of a band of "desperadoes" who had killed Deputy Sheriff Jones at Crane's. No account said whether any of the three had been tried, and none gave their race.

Masked men took Shelton, Redmond and French from the jail at Los Lunas and hanged them to the nearest trees, or, in some versions, to a single adjacent tree. The mob then took two prisoners described as "negroes" from the jail, beat them "unmercifully" and turned them loose. The dispatches gave no names for the two men, no charges against them and no reason for the beating. Neither the size of the mob nor the time of day was reported, and no jailer or officer appears in any account.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage. The last notices, in weekly papers of March 15 and 16, reduced the wire account to a sentence or two.

The first dated version was a Denver dispatch of March 8, printed that day in the St. Paul Daily Globe, and by March 9 and 10 the Republican's Albuquerque special was running in dailies from Sacramento to Portland, Maine. Headlines varied with the desk: the Washington Evening Star ran "Lynch Law in New Mexico. Three Prisoners Hanged by a Mob and Two Beaten," the Portland Daily Press "Judge Lynch," and the Tombstone Epitaph "The Avengers in New Mexico." The Wheeling Register filed the item under "Western Pastimes" and gave the beatings equal billing with "Three Men Hanged by a Mob—Two Others Badly Beaten," while the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer set it under "Deeds of Blood" and "The Amenities of Life in the Southwest."

Every version treated the accusations as settled, writing that Shelton "murdered" and Redmond "killed" their victims, and several called the three simply "murderers"; among the papers read, only the Elk County Advocate wrote "alleged murderers." Beyond the wire's word "unmercifully," no paper commented on the beating of the two Black prisoners or on the conduct of the mob. As the item was condensed for weekly news digests, its details drifted: the South Kentuckian placed the jail at Santa Fe, the Elk County Advocate at Albuquerque, and the Watertown Republican at "Los Lunas, Cal." Other printings rendered the town as "Los Tunas" or "Lastania" and the third man as "Harvey French" or "Henry French."

Dispatches dated March 8 from Albuquerque and Denver said the hanging happened "yesterday," and the Portland Daily Press said "on Tuesday," both pointing to March 7. Versions datelined March 9 also said "yesterday," which would make it March 8, the date the Batesville Guard gave, while the Pickens Sentinel said the 9th. Because the March 8 dispatches came first and the March 9 texts repeat them almost word for word, the later "yesterday" was probably carried over from the original, which makes March 7 the better-supported date.

Accounts also differ on Shelton's alleged victim, given as "Foreman Woodruff" in most versions but as "a fireman at Woodruff" in the Los Angeles Herald and "fireman Woodruff" in the Portland Daily Press. The Waco Daily Examiner put Redmond's alleged killing on the Southern Pacific rather than the Atlantic and Pacific railway.

reader.title: Lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French
bases: Masked men took three accused murderers from the Los Lunas jail and hanged them, and beat two Black prisoners from the same jail (A4, A6, A13).

Three jail prisoners accused of murder were hanged by 'masked men' or 'a mob of masked men' (A4, A13), a killing without legal authority on the pretext of punishing alleged crimes; no report gives the number in the mob, so the three-or-more element rests on the words 'mob' and 'masked men' alone.

A single Albuquerque special to the Denver Republican underlies nearly every report (A4, A9, A14), but two separately filed datelines (Denver and Albuquerque, March 8 and 9) carry it, and no report contradicts the core event (A1, A6, A2).

framing.detail: Most dailies ran the Albuquerque special verbatim, stating the three men's alleged crimes as fact.
The Washington Evening Star's headline 'Lynch Law in New Mexico. Three Prisoners Hanged by a Mob and Two Beaten' named the act as lynch law and gave the beatings a place in the headline.

Ironic or approving headings framed the hanging as frontier justice or spectacle: 'The Avengers in New Mexico', 'Western Pastimes', 'The Amenities of Life in the Southwest', 'Judge Lynch's Work in New Mexico'.
The Elk County Advocate alone called the three 'alleged murderers'.

conflicts.note: The March 8 datelines are the earliest and the March 9 texts repeat them nearly word for word, so the 'yesterday' in the later texts was probably carried over; March 7 is the better-supported date.

Los Lunas, in the dispatches filed from Albuquerque and Denver, is the original; the rest are OCR or typesetting variants and digest errors (the Albuquerque placements confuse the dateline with the jail).
Same man in the same wire text; Harry is the most common form.
Wire variants; whether Woodruff was a person or a place is unclear from the texts.
